the fibula in chick is formed from the region where Hoxd11 and Hoxd12 are expressed at the onset of limb bud development, but their expression is heterochronically terminated before the onset of cartilaginous condensation.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the avian fibula is a result of a heterochronically accelerated decline in expression of Hox11/12, which leads to a reduction in the size of the region for the fibula, and that the fibula is a structure that is produced by the region defined by Hox11/13 expression in the mouse limb bud.
the fibula is a good example to demonstrate that the morphological diversity is produced by a combination of the fixed Hox gene code and the temporal changes in expression of Hox gene.

a heterochronically earlier disappearance of Hox expression in the chick zeugopod is responsible for the short fibula, which is a peculiar trait of the avian hind limb, and that this is a morphological phenotype‐associated trait because it is not seen in the forelimb.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Hox code, which is the same in all tetrapods, can produce different morphology in different species.

the fibula in avian hindlimbs is a result of a heterochronically accelerated decline of Hoxd gene expression in the zeugopod, and this is a mechanism that produces the morphological diversity of the fibula among species.
the Hox code is not a static blueprint but rather a dynamic system that is subject to change during development.
